blocks.text: Baal Aruch gives the fourth interpretation from the book Vajekra Rabba, already cited, as follows: רבנן אמרו עוף טהור הוא ומעולא הוא והיה בא מברבריאה והיה עולה על שולחן שלמה בכל יום, Our teachers said that it is a clean and excellent bird, which was brought from Barbaria and was served daily at the table of Solomon. And Kimchi on the books of Kings: ובדברי רז״ל עוף הבא מברבריא ונקראים ברבורים על שם מקומם, In the words of our teachers of blessed memory, it was a bird brought from Barbaria, called barbur (or barbar) after the name of its place. And in the Lexicon he cites the very same words as Baal Aruch. Elias too, in the Thisbi: אומרין שהוא עוף שמן מברבריאה, They say it is a fat bird from Barbaria, and the rest, as in the others. This interpretation ought not to have been met with such hissing by the learned, as though the name Barbaria for a particular region had been born only today or yesterday. For it is supposed that the Arabs not long ago gave the name Barbaria to Numidia, or, as some hold, to the whole part of Africa that lies along the Mediterranean Sea from Egypt as far as Gades. Anyone curious about such matters will find the reasons for this name in Scaliger, Exercitation 51 against Cardano, in Leo Africanus, book 1, chapter 2, and in Marmol, Africa, book 1, chapter 6. And indeed the name Barbaria for the part of Africa we have mentioned is not to be found in Strabo, nor in Mela, nor in Pliny, nor in Marcianus, nor in Ptolemy, nor in any geographer of antiquity. Yet it is utterly false that it was given by the Arabs, since it was already current in the age of Justinian, long before the Arabs went there. Hence Anastasius Sinaita, a contemporary of Justinian, in his Anagogical Contemplations on the Hexaemeron: Ἐν τοῖς πλησιοχώροις Αἰγύπτου τοῖς ἐν Πενταπόλει τῇ Βαρβαρικῇ λεγομένοις ἀδύτοις [En tois plēsiochōrois Aigyptou tois en Pentapolei tē Barbarikē legomenois adytois]. In these words the Cyrenaic Pentapolis is placed in the Barbaria of Africa. And those whom the Vandals around that time transferred from Mount Aurasius in Mauretania to Sardinia were called Barbaricini. So testify Procopius in book 2 of the Vandal War, and Gregory, Epistles 25 and 27 of book 3. But I also find in the writings of the ancients another Barbaria, whose name is much older: namely the Ethiopian Barbaria, which is in turn twofold. One is Barbaria properly so called, the other the Troglodytic. Both [II, 701] lie along the sea: the latter along the Arabian, Adulic and Avalite gulfs, the former along the Barbaric gulf. By the name Barbaria Ptolemy and Marcianus of Heraclea understand only the former. But others also count among the Barbarians the dwellers by the Arabian Sea and the Troglodytes. Thus Arrian in the Periplus places the Barbarians and Barbaria around Berenice, Orine, the island of Diodorus, Ptolemais Theron, and the emporium of Avalites, which are places of the Troglodytica. And Stephanus, in his book On Cities, writes that Barbaria is παρὰ τὸν Ἀράβιον κόλπον [para ton Arabion kolpon], where the Troglodytica is. The Arab geographer likewise describes ارض [col. 130] بربرة [arḍ barbara], the Barbaran land, or land of Barbaria, الي البحر اليماني [ilā al-baḥr al-yamānī] towards the Yemenite sea, that is, the Arabian, Clim. 1, section 6. And in the preceding chapter he describes مدن الحبشة الساحلية [mudun al-ḥabasha al-sāḥiliyya] the coastal towns of the Abyssinians الي ما اتصل بها من عمارات البربرة [ilā mā ittaṣala bihā min ʿimārāt al-barbara] until one reaches the inhabited places of Barbaria. And Alcamus on the word بربر [barbar] Barbar: بربر جيل البرابرة وهم بالغرب وامة اخري بين الحبوش والزنج يقطعون مذاكير الرجال ويجعلونها مهور نسايهم وكلهم ولد كيس غيلان او هم بطنان من حمير صنهاجة وكتامة صاروا الي البربر ايام فتح افريقيس الملك افريقية [barbar jīl al-barābira wa-hum bi-l-gharb wa-umma ukhrā bayna al-ḥubūsh wa-l-zanj yaqṭaʿūna madhākīr al-rijāl wa-yajʿalūnahā muhūr nisāyihim wa-kulluhum walad kays ghaylān aw hum baṭnān min ḥimyar ṣanhāja wa-kutāma ṣārū ilā al-barbar ayyām fatḥ ifrīqīs al-malik ifrīqiya] Barbar, the nation of the Barbarians, who are in the west. There is also another nation between the Abyssinians and the Zinj, which cuts off men's genitals and assigns them as dowry to their wives (just as David acquired a wife for himself with a dowry of two hundred foreskins, 1 Sam. XVIII, 25. 27. and 2 Sam. III, 14.). All of them are sons of Cais Gailan, or of the stock of Humeir (from whom the Homerites are named). But Sunhagia and Cutama went into Barbaria when the African king opened up Africa. And more recent geographers too describe, in the Avalite gulf, a part of the Troglodytica, a city Barbara, or Barbora, and an island of the same name next to the city, at which Varthema says he landed after setting sail from Zeila, Navigat. book 2, ch. 16. And Duarte Barbosa has much about the same in his India, in the chapter On Barbora. From this Galen is easily reconciled with Dioscorides: the former reports that ginger is brought ἀπὸ τῆς Βαρβαρίας [apo tēs Barbarias], from Barbaria; the latter, from the Troglodytica. For Barbaria and Troglodytis are the same region. Not knowing this, Pliny misunderstood what he had read in the Greeks, that Troglodytic myrrh is also called Barbaran, as if they meant that this kind of myrrh was squalid and barbarous in appearance. For so he interprets it in book 12, chapter 16. Whereas, on the contrary, in Dioscorides it is said to be διαυγὴς [diaugēs], shining or translucent. Hence in Isidore, book 17, ch. 8, it is commended for its purity: Myrrh, he says, Troglodyte, from an island of Arabia, where a better and purer kind is gathered. Accordingly it is praised in these words in the old Hymn On the Epiphany of the Lord: Incense to God, myrrh Troglodyte for burial. For that is how it should be read, not, [II, 702] as commonly, trocletem, as Cassander rightly pointed out long ago. Troglodytic myrrh was therefore called Barbaran, not as squalid in appearance, but by reason of its native soil. Nor is there any other reason why at Gen. X, 3. the Jerusalem translator renders Thogarma as ברבריא Barbaria than a deceptive play on the names Thogarma and τρώγλην [trōglēn], whence Troglitis or Troglodytis. From this it is more than sufficiently clear that the name Barbaria comprises the whole seacoast of Eastern Ethiopia, from the borders of Egypt as far as the promontory of Rhapta. It seems to have received this name because of its uncivilized customs. Arrian: Ἀτακτότεροι δὲ οἱ κατοικοῦντες τὸν τόπον Βάρβα- [col. 131] ροι [Ataktoteroi de hoi katoikountes ton topon Barbaroi]. Or because of its barbarous and uncouth speech, if one can call speech what is more truly the squeaking of bats. Herodotus, Muse 4: Οἱ Τρωγλοδύται Αἰθίοπες γλῶσσαν οὐδεμίῃ ἄλλῃ παρομοίην νενομίκασι, ἀλλὰ τετρύγασι καθάπερ αἱ νυκτερίδες [Hoi Trōglodytai Aithiopes glōssan oudemiē allē paromoiēn nenomikasi, alla tetrygasi kathaper hai nykterides]. Pliny, book 5, ch. 8: Their (food) is the flesh of serpents, and they have a squeak, not a voice: so wholly do they lack the exchange of speech. Martianus Capella, book 6: They squeak rather than speak. As Solinus: Ignorant of speech, they squeak rather than speak. Rightly, then, were they called Barbarians. For properly so are called οἱ δυσεκφόρως, καὶ σκληρῶς, καὶ τραχέως λαλοῦντες [hoi dysekphorōs, kai sklērōs, kai tracheōs lalountes], as Strabo shows at length on that verse of Homer ^{e)} in which he calls the Carians Βαρβαροφώνους [Barbarophōnous]. In this very sense the Greek, Chaldee, Arabic and Latin translators at Psal. CXIV, 1. call barbarous the people which the Hebrews call עם לועז. For to the Hebrews לועז is one who speaks a foreign tongue, and that absurd and uncouth. Nor do the lexicographers of the Arabs explain بربار [barbār] barbar otherwise. Giggeius: بربار [barbār] (barbar) garrulous, making a din, clamouring. بربرة [barbara] (barbara) the bleating of goats, triviality, the speech of an angry man, which is usually abrupt with ill-articulated words, as it is in Seneca. Golius: بربر [barbara] (barbara, verb) he grumbled as angry men do: which is taken from Giauhari. But Alcamus preceded Giggeius; his words are: البربرة صوت المعز وكثرة الكلام والجلبة والصياح [al-barbara ṣawt al-maʿz wa-kathrat al-kalām wa-l-jalaba wa-l-ṣiyāḥ] (Albarbara) the voice of the goat, much talking, clamour and shouting. Therefore the name Barbaria was as much Chaldee and Arabic as Greek, and so was very well known to the Jews and Syrians, in whose books it occurs everywhere. Examples from the Talmud and the paraphrasts are found in Baal Aruch; from the Ielammedenu in Buxtorf; from Semoth Rabba and Esther Rabba in David Cohen de Lara. To these I add from Gorionides, on Aretas, king of the Arabs, about to fight against Herod, book 5, ch. 18 and 19: He gathers all his army, the army, that is, of Arabia, וצבא ברבר, and the army of barbaria. And shortly after, the Jews bring back much spoil from the Arabs, ומן ברבר, and from the Barbarians. In that age, of course, part of Barbaria was subject to the rule of the Arabs. Indeed even the more remote Barbarians [II, 703] as far as Rhapta acknowledged the kings of Arabia Felix as their lords. Hence Arrian on Rhapta and the region around Rhapta: Νέμεται δὲ αὐτὴν κατά τι δίκαιον ἀρχαῖον, ὑποπίπτουσαν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῆς πρώτης γινομένης Ἀραβίας, ὁ Μωφαρίτης τύραννος [Nemetai de autēn kata ti dikaion archaion, hypopiptousan tē basileia tēs prōtēs ginomenēs Arabias, ho Mōpharitēs tyrannos]· The Mopharite tyrant possesses it, subject by some ancient right to the kingdom of the first Arabia. I think the same Barbarians are meant by the Talmudists when, in the tractate Iebamoth, fol. 63b, they say that the foolish people of whom Moses speaks in Deut. XXXII, 21. are אנשי ברבריא שמהלכין ערומין בשוק, the men of Barbaria, who walk naked through the streets. For they were either naked or half-covered with a hide. Dionysius on the Erembi, or Troglodytes, verse 965.
